findings.title: Up to 6 attempts reach db per request
findings.detail: Retries multiply along the path: 2 × 3 = 6 (clients (client) ×2, api→db ×3). When db is failing, it receives 6× the traffic exactly when it is weakest.
findings.suggestion: Retry at one layer only (usually the outermost), use a retry budget, and fail fast below it.

findings.title: api retries db immediately
findings.detail: 3 attempts with 0 ms backoff: when db struggles, retries arrive at once and add load exactly when it can least absorb it.
findings.suggestion: Use exponential backoff with jitter (e.g. 50–100 ms base) and a retry budget.

findings.title: clients retry without backoff
findings.detail: Clients retry 2 times immediately after a failure or timeout, multiplying load during an incident.
findings.suggestion: Add exponential backoff with jitter on the client.

findings.title: db has no replica
findings.detail: A primary failure is an outage for every read and write that reaches it.
findings.suggestion: Add a standby or read replicas (relational), a replica set (document stores) or replication factor 3 (wide-column).

findings.title: No rate limit at the edge
findings.detail: Nothing in front of the system caps traffic, so a spike, a retry storm or a bot flood reaches every tier at full force.
findings.suggestion: Add a rate limit on the gateway or load balancer sized to the capacity you have measured.

findings.title: api cannot scale out
findings.detail: Autoscaling is on but the maximum (3) is not above the minimum (3), so no capacity can be added under load.
findings.suggestion: Raise maxReplicas to cover the expected peak (for example 3× the baseline).

findings.title: No rate limit at the edge

findings.title: api scales late
findings.detail: Target utilization 90% leaves little headroom while new replicas start (30 s); a spike saturates the existing ones first.
findings.suggestion: Target 50–70% utilization for latency-sensitive services, or keep warm spare capacity.

findings.title: queue has an unbounded backlog
findings.detail: If consumers fall behind or a downstream dependency is down, queue keeps accepting messages without limit (memory, disk and recovery time grow).
findings.suggestion: Set a maximum depth or retention and alert on consumer lag; decide what producers do when it is full.

findings.title: queue runs on one broker
findings.detail: Producers cannot publish while the only broker of queue is down, so the asynchronous path stops with it.
findings.suggestion: Run 3 brokers with replicated partitions/queues, or use a managed queue.

findings.title: No rate limit at the edge
findings.detail: Nothing in front of the system caps traffic, so a spike, a retry storm or a bot flood reaches every tier at full force.
findings.suggestion: Add a rate limit on the gateway or load balancer sized to the capacity you have measured.

findings.title: api waits indefinitely on queue
findings.detail: No timeout on queue: a slow or hung dependency keeps api's workers waiting until its pool fills and requests queue behind them.
findings.suggestion: Set per-call timeouts a little above each dependency's p99 (for example 2× p99), keeping their sum inside the caller's own budget.

findings.title: 3 consumers of queue sit idle
findings.detail: Only one consumer per partition is active: 2 partitions cap parallelism at 2 although 5 consumers run.
findings.suggestion: Add partitions or reduce consumers.

findings.title: queue has no downstream link
findings.detail: Consumers process messages but call nothing, so the asynchronous work is not modelled beyond the queue.
findings.suggestion: Link the queue's output to the service or store its consumers write to.

findings.title: api waits indefinitely on payments
findings.detail: No timeout on payments: a slow or hung dependency keeps api's workers waiting until its pool fills and requests queue behind them.
findings.suggestion: Set per-call timeouts a little above each dependency's p99 (for example 2× p99), keeping their sum inside the caller's own budget.

findings.title: 5.0% of calls to payments fail
findings.detail: api call payments once with no retry, so every transient upstream error becomes a user-visible failure.
findings.suggestion: Add one retry with backoff and jitter for idempotent calls, or a fallback/queue for non-critical calls.

findings.title: Reads fail when cache is down
findings.detail: api reads db on a cache miss, but a failed lookup on cache fails the read instead of counting as a miss.
findings.suggestion: Turn on 'Carry on if this call fails' on the link to cache and give api a link to the data store set to 'Reads only on a cache miss', so reads fall back to the data store (check it can take every read), or run the cache with replicas.

findings.title: db lets requests wait forever
findings.detail: db has no connection acquire timeout, so up to 200 requests can wait with no limit while clients have long given up.
findings.suggestion: Set a queue timeout below the caller's timeout so stale work is shed early.

findings.title: api can open 1,000 connections to db

findings.suggestion: Put a connection pooler or proxy in front (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy-style), or cap function concurrency.

findings.title: db's hot data does not fit in memory
findings.detail: 75% of 2 GiB is buffer cache for about 5 GiB of hot data per instance, so about 70% of reads go to disk.
findings.suggestion: Give each instance more memory, shard the data, or cache the hottest reads in front.

findings.title: db may have a hot shard
findings.detail: Key popularity follows Zipf s=0.99: the most popular keys land on a few of the 2 shards, so the hottest shard can get several times its fair 50.0% share. Simulate to measure it.
findings.suggestion: Pick a higher-cardinality partition key, cache hot keys, or split hot keys across partitions.

findings.title: orders's hot data does not fit in memory
findings.detail: 75% of 8 GiB is buffer cache for about 9.5 GiB of hot data per instance, so about 37% of reads go to disk.
findings.suggestion: Give each instance more memory, shard the data, or cache the hottest reads in front.

findings.title: api needs more CPU at peak

findings.suggestion: Give it more CPU cores or replicas, or reduce the CPU work per request.

findings.title: Up to 16 attempts reach s4x5 per request
findings.detail: Retries multiply along the path: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 (s0x0→s1x5 ×2, s1x5→s2x5 ×2, s2x5→s3x5 ×2, s3x5→s4x5 ×2). When s4x5 is failing, it receives 16× the traffic exactly when it is weakest.
findings.suggestion: Retry at one layer only (usually the outermost), use a retry budget, and fail fast below it.

findings.title: 6 synchronous hops on one request path
findings.detail: clients → s0x0 → s1x0 → s2x0 → s3x0 → s4x0 → s5x0: every hop adds latency and its own failure probability to the request.
findings.suggestion: Collapse hops, call independent dependencies in parallel, or move non-critical work to a queue.

findings.title: clients gives up before api does
findings.detail: clients (client timeout) waits 3,000 ms for api, but api may wait up to 3,150 ms on db (1,000 ms × 3 attempts + backoff): it keeps working on requests nobody is waiting for.
findings.suggestion: Make timeouts shrink downstream (each caller waits longer than its callee's whole budget) or propagate deadlines.

findings.title: No rate limit at the edge
findings.detail: Nothing in front of the system caps traffic, so a spike, a retry storm or a bot flood reaches every tier at full force.
findings.suggestion: Add a rate limit on the gateway or load balancer sized to the capacity you have measured.

findings.title: db has no replica
findings.detail: A primary failure is an outage for every read and write that reaches it.
findings.suggestion: Add a standby or read replicas (relational), a replica set (document stores) or replication factor 3 (wide-column).

findings.title: clients gives up before api does
findings.detail: clients (client timeout) waits 1,000 ms for api, but api may wait up to 2,550 ms on db (800 ms × 3 attempts + backoff): it keeps working on requests nobody is waiting for.
findings.suggestion: Make timeouts shrink downstream (each caller waits longer than its callee's whole budget) or propagate deadlines.

findings.title: solo runs on one broker
findings.detail: Producers cannot publish while the only broker of solo is down, so the asynchronous path stops with it.
findings.suggestion: Run 3 brokers with replicated partitions/queues, or use a managed queue.

findings.title: db may have a hot shard
findings.detail: Key popularity follows Zipf s=0.99: the most popular keys land on a few of the 4 shards, so the hottest shard can get several times its fair 25.0% share. Simulate to measure it.
findings.suggestion: Pick a higher-cardinality partition key, cache hot keys, or split hot keys across partitions.

findings.title: db uses consistency ALL
findings.detail: Every operation waits for all 3 replicas: latency follows the slowest one and a single replica outage fails the request.
findings.suggestion: Use QUORUM for both reads and writes to keep strong consistency with one replica down.

findings.title: api runs a single replica
findings.detail: One crash, deploy or host failure takes down every request that passes through api (autoscaling minimum is 1).
findings.suggestion: Run at least 2 replicas (3 across zones for critical paths) behind the load balancer.

findings.title: Reads fail when cache is down
findings.detail: Every read from api goes through cache; if the cache itself is unavailable, reads have no other path.
findings.suggestion: Turn on 'Carry on if this call fails' on the link to cache and give api a link to the data store set to 'Reads only on a cache miss', so reads fall back to the data store (check it can take every read), or run the cache with replicas.

findings.title: db has fewer connections than callers
findings.detail: Up to 40 blocking workers (api) can wait on db, which accepts 10 connections. When it slows down, 30 requests queue for a connection.
findings.suggestion: Size application pools to the database's real concurrency, add a pooler, or cap service concurrency.

findings.title: cache assumes a 99.0% hit ratio
findings.detail: Hit ratios this high are rare outside static content; the data store behind it is sized for the misses you assume.
findings.suggestion: Use the measured hit ratio, or the TTL + keyspace model, and test a cold-cache scenario.

findings.title: lb is a single instance
findings.detail: lb is modelled as one self-hosted instance; if it stops, nothing behind it is reachable.
findings.suggestion: Run two instances with failover (floating IP, DNS) or use a managed load balancer.

findings.title: db lets requests wait forever
findings.detail: db has no connection acquire timeout, so up to 0 requests can wait with no limit while clients have long given up.
findings.suggestion: Set a queue timeout below the caller's timeout so stale work is shed early.

findings.title: api retries ghost immediately
findings.detail: 2 attempts with 0 ms backoff: when ghost struggles, retries arrive at once and add load exactly when it can least absorb it.
findings.suggestion: Use exponential backoff with jitter (e.g. 50–100 ms base) and a retry budget.

findings.title: worker needs more CPU at peak
findings.detail: At the 100 req/s peak about 100 req/s reach worker; 0.1 vCPU × 1 replica at 10.0 ms of CPU work per request handle about 10 req/s, so its CPU would be 1000% busy and requests queue for a core. This is a static estimate (first attempts, fixed hit ratios); a run measures it.
findings.suggestion: Give it more CPU cores or replicas, or reduce the CPU work per request.

findings.title: orders's hot data does not fit in memory
findings.detail: 75% of 1 GiB is buffer cache for about 100 GiB of hot data per instance, so about 99% of reads go to disk.
findings.suggestion: Give each instance more memory, shard the data, or cache the hottest reads in front.

findings.title: cache holds 27,962 of 1,000,000 keys
findings.detail: 80% of 0.1 GiB fits about 27,962 items of 3 KiB; the least recently used keys are evicted, so expect a lower hit ratio than with unbounded memory.
findings.suggestion: Add memory if the hit ratio matters, or shorten what you cache.
